Moi, @mirokarv, thank you for your detailed input and proposals.

I don't comment on proposals from the technical side, but more from a ASVS requirement buildup side.

If we have a requirement for something already (e.g., PAR must be used), it is good to have technical conditions in the same requirement. As PAR is mentioned in 3 requirements, it is a bit more complicated task.

Proposals are detailed (as there are many aspects to cover) and lead to the implementation guide area. An ASVS requirement should be more focused on the security weakness to cover - an ideal requirement is self-explanatory, what security problem it addresses. It may get lengthy and to cover many situations, 10.4.5 can be example for such requirement.

I'm not a big fan of the idea of pointing to external resources in a requirement text, such as an RFC, but we have done it for some requirements (5.4.2), and it may work in this situation. As rules for PAR and JAR are written in separate specifications, we may point to those specifications.

> Where upstream RFCs use the MUST keyword, that's already part of the protocol and therefore non-compliant implementations aren't really using JAR/PAR. 

I think that many requirements in the documents are checks of requirements of the related protocol standards. Au auditor would still need to check that these requirements are actually (and properly) implemented. Moreover many requirements from existing protocol standards do not have a direct security impact and are not relevant here.

***

> Verify that when PAR is used, the authorization server binds each request_uri to the client_id of the client that created it. A request_uri issued for one client must be rejected when presented by a different client.

I would say that this is not really specific to PAR. I'd claim that  

A related topic is:

> 10.4.10 Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client‑to‑authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.

What may be lacking in the context of PAR is the requirement that the `client_id` in the PAR body maps to the authenticated client (eg. if using a client assertion, basic authentication, TLS authentication, etc.).

***

> Verify that when PAR is used, the authorization server treats request_uri values as one-time use and rejects expired request_uri values. The lifetime of the request_uri (expires_in) must be short, typically ≤ 90 seconds and must not exceed 600 seconds.

Yes, this might be needed. I am wondering if it would make sense to include it into a more general requirement about short-lived AS state in general in order to avoid creating too many requirements.

***

> Verify that when JAR is used, the authorization server requires a unique jti claim in the request object and enforces replay protection by rejecting previously used jti values within the object's validity period. Verify that the request object contains an exp claim with a short lifetime.

For me, using `jti` is implementation detail and if a requirement is needed, it should be more general about implementing replay protection. For example, an implementation could use a cryptographic hash of the token to more reliably identify the token for replay protection purpose.

Another issue, is that the [example from RFC 9101](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9101#name-request-object) does not event include the `jti` claim.

I believe that a more critical requirement would be to verify that that the client actually includes an (short-lived) expiration in the JAR JWT (as well as `nbf` and `iat` claims).. I do not believe this requirement is already covered anywhere else. (And a replay protection would face important scalability issues if the token does not include expiration.)

***

> Verify that when JAR is used (standalone or inside PAR), the client_id value in the authorization request query parameter exactly matches the client_id claim inside the signed request object.

This might better be part of a more general requirement about protecting against cross-client / client confusion attacks:

* when client authentication is used (eg. PAR), the authenticated client must match with the client on the request (if any).

This should arguably part of a more general requirement about authorization in general which would be an argument against having an explicit requirement about this.

***

> Verify that when PAR or JAR is used, the authorization server does not allow query string parameters on the /authorize endpoint to override values contained in the pushed request or request object. The server must only use parameters from the request object / pushed data.

Same thing here. I agree this is important but on the other hand this could be seen as a general requirement about request confusion ambiguity.

I would formulate something like:

> Verify that when the authorization request is secured (such as with PAR or JAR), the authorization server does not accept unverified request parameters or override existing request parameters (eg. by adding them in the query string).

Nitpick: when using OIDC, the request parameter could be passed in the request body, not only in the request parameter.
